title: Chapter 11: Exceptions, Validation, and Failure Design
description: Treat failures as API behavior rather than afterthoughts. Learners choose checked or unchecked semantics from caller recovery, translate infrastructure errors without losing causes, read cause and suppressed chains, establish resource ownership with try-with-resources, and design validation and user messages that aid correction without exposing sensitive internals.

lessons.title: Throwable hierarchy and checked versus unchecked exceptions

exercises.title: Throwable hierarchy and checked versus unchecked exceptions: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Which failure must generally be caught or declared by a caller?
hints: Checked exceptions declared with throws must be caught or declared by the caller; RuntimeException and Error carry no such compiler-enforced obligation.

lessons.title: Throwing domain-specific failures and preserving causes

exercises.title: Throwing domain-specific failures and preserving causes: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why retain the original exception as a cause?
choices: To preserve diagnostic evidence across abstraction translation
hints: The cause constructor parameter links the new exception to the original one so its message and stack trace remain reachable through getCause() after translation.

lessons.title: Catching, propagation, multi-catch, and reading stack traces

exercises.title: Catching, propagation, multi-catch, and reading stack traces: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why narrow a try block around parsing?
choices: Unrelated failures should not be mislabeled as invalid text
A broader catch(Exception) block runs measurably slower than catching NumberFormatException directly
Exceptions disappear outside a try block
hints: A try block scoped to just the parsing call keeps a defect in process() from being caught and mislabeled as a parsing failure.

exercises.title: try-with-resources, ownership, and suppressed exceptions: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: If both the body and close fail in try-with-resources, which failure is primary?
choices: The close failure always replaces the body
The body's failure, with close failure suppressed
hints: try-with-resources keeps the body's failure as primary and attaches any exception thrown by close() as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed().

lessons.title: Boundary validation and safe user-facing error reporting

exercises.title: Boundary validation and safe user-facing error reporting: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Does valid input prove that the caller is authorized?
choices: No; authorization is a separate check
hints: Passing syntactic and semantic validation says nothing about who the caller is; authorization is a separate check performed independently of the parsed value.

exercises.title: Exceptions, Validation, and Failure Design: professional judgment
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A storage outage is converted to an empty result. What is lost?
choices: The distinction between absence and failure
The specific exception type that caused the outage

exercises.title: Chapter 11 implementation lab: parsePort
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `parsePort`. Parse a decimal port from 1 through 65535; return -1 for malformed or out-of-range text. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Use Integer.parseInt spelling rules with no whitespace trimming, then require 1..65535. Malformed and out-of-range values return -1.
hints: Decide separately whether the text is a syntactically valid decimal integer (Integer.parseInt, no trimming) and whether the parsed value falls within 1..65535.
Check the boundaries 0, 1, 65535, and 65536, plus malformed and whitespace-padded text, before submitting.

exercises.title: Preserve the original cause
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the exception translation so the caught NumberFormatException is passed as the cause of the thrown IllegalArgumentException, and the program writes exactly `true`. Keep the two-exception structure and explain why forwarding the cause makes the getCause() check pass, rather than hard-coding the print statement. Output tests verify the printed result; confirming the cause is genuinely preserved requires reading the source.
hints: Pass the caught exception as the translated exception's cause.
